conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m the medicine doctor taking care of you tonight. I understand you came in for worsening left upper abdominal pain near your G-tube site. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s the same pain I’ve had for months, but the last two weeks it’s been getting worse. Tonight it got unbearable. It’s right here by the tube and it shoots to my left side.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Is it tied to your tube feeds—like it flares when the feeds are running? Any vomiting, diarrhea, fevers, or blood in stool?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It gets worse when the feeds are going in. I’ve been dry heaving sometimes, but no real vomiting. No fever, no diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. In the emergency department your vitals were stable, and your bloodwork—CBC, electrolytes, and lipase—looked normal. We also got a chest X-ray to look for free air under the diaphragm, and it did not show any free air.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a perforation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Right—based on your exam and that X-ray, we don’t see signs of a perforation. Your belly exam is reassuring too—no guarding or rebound, and the tube site doesn’t look infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Then why does it hurt so much? I’m scared something is wrong with the tube.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your history, the bariatric surgery team thinks this is most likely pain from your known marginal ulcer, and possibly irritation around the tube site—especially if it’s been manipulated a lot. They don’t recommend more imaging or any surgical intervention tonight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They’re not going to do anything? I can’t live like this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We are going to treat your pain and keep you safe. You got IV Dilaudid in the ED and it helped. Our plan is to control pain here, keep your ulcer medicines going—lansoprazole dissolvable and sucralfate through the tube—and restart your continuous tube feeds as you can tolerate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My feeds were off because it hurt too much. I’m worried my sugar will crash.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a real concern with your post-bypass hypoglycemia. In the ED you were supported with dextrose fluids while feeds were off. Now that you’re here, we’ll restart your continuous tube feeds and monitor your glucose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But what if the tube is infected? It feels sore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam there’s no redness, warmth, drainage that looks infected, or swelling around the tube. Your white blood cell count is normal as well. We’ll keep checking it, but right now there’s no evidence of infection causing the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: how is your pain after the medication? Any new nausea or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s better than when I came in. Still there, but not as sharp. No vomiting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your morning labs look stable—blood counts and electrolytes are in a good range, and your glucose this morning was normal. How did you do overnight with the tube feeds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They restarted them and I didn’t have a low sugar episode. The pain still flares when it runs, but it’s manageable with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That matches what we’re seeing. Since there’s no sign of obstruction or infection and surgery doesn’t think more testing is needed right now, the focus is symptom control and continuing ulcer treatment. You still have the plan for an EGD at the end of the month, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s scheduled. Will that actually help figure this out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can. The scope lets your team directly look at the gastrojejunal area and assess the marginal ulcer. In the meantime, staying consistent with lansoprazole and sucralfate is important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What am I going home with for pain? The pills don’t always absorb right with my bypass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re discharging you with liquid oxycodone to use as needed for pain, which can be given through the G-tube. We also want you to follow up with a pain management clinic to talk about longer-term strategies, since this has been going on for months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m nervous about taking opioids. And I’m already on lorazepam and Ambien.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s an important point. Use the oxycodone only as prescribed and only when you need it. Because sedating medicines can add up, avoid extra doses of lorazepam or Ambien beyond what you normally take, and don’t drive or do anything risky while you’re using the oxycodone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you go, let’s review: continue your continuous tube feeds to prevent hypoglycemia, keep taking lansoprazole and sucralfate for the marginal ulcer, and watch the tube site for redness, swelling, pus-like drainage, fever, or worsening pain. If any of those happen, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll keep the feeds running and take the ulcer meds. I’ll follow up with pain clinic and keep my scope appointment. Thank you.
